title: Analyze Mixture Design
modelname: Model Name (leave blank for an automatic name)
linearChk: Linear Scheff model - main effects only
quadChk: Quadratic Scheff model - main effects + all pairwise component interactions
cubicChk: Special Cubic Scheff model - quadratic + all three-way component products
lblModelTypeNote: Full Cubic Scheff models are not supported in this dialog.
showLofChk: Show lack-of-fit test (requires replicated design points)
showContourPlotChk: Show ternary plot of the fitted model (color-filled surface)
plotComponents: For designs with MORE than 3 components: select exactly 3 to plot (others held at their mean observed value). Ignored when exactly 3 components were selected above.
showDesignPointsChk: Overlay actual design points on the ternary plot

help.title: Analyze Mixture Design
help.r_help: No external mixture-specific package required — fits with lm() and plots with ggplot2.
help.body:
Description
Fits a Scheffé canonical mixture model (Linear, Quadratic, or Special Cubic) to the results of a mixture experiment, using lm() with the correct no-intercept parameterization, reports a corrected R² appropriate for mixture models, lack-of-fit, residual diagnostics, and a ternary plot (a color-filled surface, not contour lines) of the fitted response surface.

Why mixture models have no intercept
Because mixture components always sum to a fixed total, an ordinary intercept term is mathematically redundant — Scheffé canonical models omit it and instead let every component's own coefficient carry the predicted response at that component's pure vertex. This dialog fits models of exactly this no-intercept form automatically; you do not need to specify it yourself.

Why R² is corrected
R's own lm() computes R² differently for a no-intercept model: by default it is calculated relative to the raw sum of squares of the response (Σy²) rather than the sum of squares around the mean (Σ(y−ȳ)²), which produces an artificially inflated value that is not comparable to R² from an ordinary model. This dialog reports both the standard lm() value and a corrected R²/adjusted R² computed relative to Σ(y−ȳ)², matching standard mixture design practice.

Model Types
  • Linear: y = Σ βᵢ xᵢ — estimates only how far each pure component's response differs from the others.
  • Quadratic: y = Σ βᵢ xᵢ + Σ βᵢⱼ xᵢ xⱼ — adds a term for every pair of components, capturing blending non-linearity. The most commonly used mixture model.
  • Special Cubic: Quadratic + Σ βᵢⱼₖ xᵢ xⱼ xₖ — adds one three-way product term for every triple of components, capturing three-way blending effects. Requires a design (e.g., a {q,3} Simplex Lattice) that supports this model order.
Two model objects are created
  • The named model — the fitted lm object, reported with both standard and corrected statistics.
  • A companion <name>_lm object (identical to the named model) — use this for prediction and optimization under MODEL EVALUATION on the main menu bar, kept for consistency with other DOE analysis dialogs.
Lack-of-fit test
Only computable when the design includes two or more runs at the exact same component proportions (replicates). Compares the fitted model's residual variation against the pure error estimated from those replicates.

Ternary plot
Ternary (triangular) plots can only display 3 components at a time. For a 3-component mixture this is automatic. For more than 3 components, select exactly 3 to plot — the remaining components are held fixed at their mean observed proportion (a "slice" through the higher-dimensional mixture space), and the 3 plotted components are shown as proportions of their own subtotal. For a 2-component mixture, a simple response vs. proportion line plot is shown instead.
